issues.issue: A "complete inventory of the lost, damaged and destroyed property" is required without any materiality qualifier or stated consequence for an imperfect inventory. Whether an incomplete inventory forfeits the claim is left open.

The duty applies "as often as may reasonably be required," and the item is printed with orphan subparagraph letters detaching a. and b. from their text. Both the frequency standard and the list structure are indeterminate.

The examination-under-oath duty extends to "any of your agents, employees, or representatives involved in the purchase of this insurance or the preparation of your claim," a class the insured may not control, yet non-compliance is a breach of the policy. Whom the insured must produce is left uncertain.

The ninety-day sworn Proof of Loss requirement runs "from the date of loss," which in a storm claim may precede discovery, and no consequence of late submission is stated. Whether the requirement is a condition precedent to payment is not said in the text.

"A sudden, fortuitous event" is set against exclusions for "any other gradually developing condition" and for conditions correctable by maintenance, leaving no line between a sudden accident and a gradual failure that finally manifests. "Sudden" carries both a temporal and an unexpectedness sense.

"Replacement cost less deduction for depreciation" does not say what may be depreciated — materials only, or labor and overhead as well — a point that decides the size of every actual cash value payment. The formula is stated without any method.

Average daily value is computed on "the number of operating days in that period," a term the policy nowhere defines, and is applied to "the entire covered location whether or not the loss effects the entire covered location." The multiplier for a partial-location loss is therefore contestable.

Business income is "gross earnings ... less all charges and expenses which do not necessarily continue," with no test for necessity of continuation, and the PAYROLL EXPENSE endorsement (c310, c311) separately limits payroll to ninety business days. What continuing expenses are included is left open between them.

"Those locations shown on the Schedule of the DECLARATIONS" is circular here, because the Schedule (c028) shows no locations and instead says "All covered locations as per Statement of Values on file with us." The definition therefore does not identify any location by itself.

The definition can also not be squared with the DECLARATIONS Schedule note that "Insurance does not apply at locations ... unless a specific value is provided by you" (c028), which makes coverage depend on the insured's reporting rather than on what the Schedule shows. Which document fixes covered locations is the question.

"Covered loss" is confined to loss "at a covered location," although the Insuring Agreement (c009) and COVERAGES A. and B. (c029, c030) extend to property within 1,000 feet of, or in transit away from, a covered location. The definition and those grants describe different geographic reach.

"Covered property means property insured by this policy" defines the term by the conclusion it is used to reach, so it supplies no independent content. Every coverage grant that turns on "covered property" inherits that circularity.

"Other equipment capable of receiving, processing, storing or retrieving information" is a catch-all after a list of computer hardware, wide enough to capture ordinary machinery with embedded controls. What falls within the class is exactly the general-versus-specific question.

"Earth movement ... includes but is not limited to" four listed events, so the excluded class is open-ended, and it is not said whether man-made settling or soil shifting under a structure counts. The catch-all against the enumerated causes is the defect.

Extra expense is limited to costs to continue the business "as nearly normal as practicable," with "normal" defined only by reference to the condition that would have existed had no loss happened. The standard gives no way to measure which extra costs qualify.

"Property of rarity, antiquity, or artistic merit, including but not limited to" a long list makes the class open-ended and the qualifying criteria subjective. Whether an item is of sufficient "artistic merit" is undefined.

"Flood" is defined to include "surface water, rain accumulation or runoff" and spray, wording broad enough to capture ordinary rainwater entering a damaged roof. Where wind or hail opens a building and rain follows, the definition's reach against the coverage grant is contestable.

Hail is defined as stones "ranging in size from pea to softball or larger," which sets a lower bound excluding smaller hail and is stated in imprecise comparative terms. Whether a storm produced qualifying "hail" turns on a size test the policy states only by analogy.

"Miscellaneous location" is defined only as a location that is not a covered, new or unscheduled location and not one "for which coverage is found, in whole or in part, elsewhere in this policy," so its content depends entirely on the contested definitions of the other categories. Any location could be argued into or out of the class.

"Machinery and equipment principally used by you or your employees away from a covered location" turns on "principally," with no measure of how much off-premises use is required. Whether an item is mobile equipment or ordinary personal property changes both the limit and the valuation basis.

"Any storm or weather disturbance that is named by the U.S. National Weather Service" identifies a naming authority that does not itself name storms, so the trigger for the wind deductible may have no referent. Whether an unnamed severe thunderstorm or hailstorm is a "Named Storm" is left unresolved.

"Equipment ... that generates, transmits or utilizes energy" is extremely broad while the exclusions strip out structure, foundations, ductwork and piping, leaving the boundary of an "object" unclear for building systems. The subparagraph letters of the exclusion list are also missing in the delivered text.

"All loss or damage attributable directly or indirectly to one (1) cause or series of similar causes" aggregated "irrespective of the amount of time or area over which such loss or damage occurs" gives no limit on how far apart in time separate storms can be and still be one occurrence. The number of occurrences, and so of deductibles and limits, turns on that undefined phrase.

"Perils insured against means causes of loss for which this policy provides coverage" defines the term by the very question it is used to answer, giving the phrase no independent content. Every grant conditioned on a "peril insured against" inherits that circularity.

The period ends when the property "using reasonable speed" could be repaired and "made ready for operations," a hypothetical measure with no benchmark, and the numbered subparagraphs are broken across the page in the delivered text. When the period ends is left to be argued from an undefined standard.

"Any covered property subject to deterioration or impairment as a result of a change in conditions including but not limited to temperature, humidity or pressure" is broad enough to cover most stock. The open-ended "change in conditions" has no limiting principle.

The three-part definition is printed without its numbering for the first two items and with a block of page and heading text inserted mid-definition, so the list cannot be read as drafted. The class of "personal property of others" is obscured by that mechanical defect.

"Policy period means the time during which insurance is provided by this policy" is circular and does not tie to the dates in the DECLARATIONS (c007). The definition supplies no independent boundary for the many provisions that turn on the policy period.

"Any solid, liquid, gaseous or thermal irritant or contaminant, including, but not limited to" a long list, with an express exception only for ammonia, is broad enough to reach ordinary building materials and debris. The reach of the pollution exclusion depends entirely on that undefined breadth.

"Buildings and any other structure" including "permanent fittings or fixtures" and "yard fixtures" does not say where real property ends and personal property or excluded items such as pavement and land begin. For roof, pavement and outdoor items the classification decides which limit and exclusion apply.

Replacement cost here "excludes any increased cost of repair or reconstruction by reason of any law or ordinance," while EXTENSIONS B. 6. (c095) grants exactly those increased construction and building-law costs when a sublimit is shown. The definition and that extension state opposite results.

"Specified perils" includes "wind or hail," both separately defined (c256, c226) in terms — air movement "at any velocity" and stones from "pea to softball" — that do not fit the narrower notion of a specified peril. Which meaning applies where an extension turns on a specified peril must be worked out across the definitions.

Unscheduled locations are those "reported to us, but not shown on the Schedule of the DECLARATIONS," yet the Schedule shows no individual locations at all and insures by reference to a Statement of Values (c028). On that reading every reported location could be an unscheduled location, for which the Declarations show "$No Coverage".

"Wind means the direct action of the movement of air at any velocity" has no lower bound, so any air movement associated with a loss is wind. That definition drives the Named Storm deductible and the specified-perils list without any limiting content.

"You and your(s) mean the named insured shown on the DECLARATIONS," which names only Great Plains Ventures Inc, while the ADDITIONAL NAMED INSURED endorsement (c259, c263) adds eight other entities as named insureds. Whose property is "your real property," and who may sue and must perform the conditions, turns on reconciling the two.

This provides insurance to each scheduled additional named insured although DEFINITIONS V.V. (c257) confines "you" and "your" to the named insured shown on the Declarations. Whether the scheduled entities' property is "your" property for purposes of the coverage grants is left unresolved between the two.

"We will adjust any covered loss only with you" narrows the adjustment right while CONDITIONS W. (c186, c187) permits adjustment with owners of property of others and CONDITIONS L. requires joint adjustment considerations with a loss payee. Who may adjust a loss involving another entity's property is stated differently in the two places.

Payment must be made "jointly to you and any person or organization shown on the Schedule," which cuts against the same endorsement's rule that loss is adjusted only with the named insured (c260) and against CONDITIONS W. 2. Who is entitled to receive proceeds is not settled by these provisions read together.

The Schedule gives the additional named insureds' location as "Per statement of values on file with us," and lists entities (for example 3526 North Oliver, LP) whose addresses do not appear in the DECLARATIONS list of locations (c028). Whether property of a scheduled entity at an unlisted address is insured cannot be answered from the policy itself.

The limits are stacked as "we will not pay more than: A ... B ... or C," joined by "or," so it is unclear whether the schedule limit and the per-item caps apply cumulatively or as alternatives. The $1,000,000 occurrence cap that follows repeats the schedule figure without resolving that.

Reporting is due "at the time you report the values at risk, or at expiration or cancellation of this policy, whichever occurs first," with no stated consequence of failing to report. Whether the coverage is lost or merely repriced is not addressed.

The replacement cost box is left unmarked while the Schedule states a $1,000,000 limit, so mobile equipment appears to fall to actual cash value under VALUATIONS B. (c131) despite the policy's general replacement cost basis (c013). Which valuation applies to this endorsement's coverage is unresolved.

This buys back only "sudden earth movement," while GROUP A exclusion 2. (c102) excludes earth movement "whether sudden or gradual." Which losses fall in the restored band depends on a sudden/gradual line neither provision draws.

The seventy-two hour aggregation rule here differs from DEFINITIONS Z. Occurrence (c235), which aggregates all loss from one cause or series of similar causes without any time limit. Which occurrence rule governs an earth movement sequence must be resolved between the two.

The limit is "the lesser of the applicable limit of liability shown on" four different documents, without saying what to do when one of them shows no figure for the loss in question. The comparison is indeterminate where a document is silent.

The percentage machinery depends on "the deductible factor shown on the Schedule of this endorsement," but that Schedule states only flat $50,000 deductibles and no factors. The mechanism has no input to operate on.

The list of coverages excluded from earth movement cover includes Form RM1112, a form not listed on the POLICY INDEX or attached to this policy. The exclusion refers to something not part of the instrument.

The lettering of the excluded areas is corrupted ("Af = op aw >") and item H. offers "Any other location(s) shown below: Not Applicable," so the enumeration cannot be read as drafted. Which locations are excluded is obscured by the mechanical defect.

This grants flood coverage at scheduled locations although GROUP A exclusion 3. (c103) excludes flood generally, and the flood Schedule (c294) is printed with its location groups detached from the corresponding limits. Which locations enjoy the buy-back is not clear from the two read together.
The seventy-two hour flood aggregation conflicts with the open-ended aggregation in DEFINITIONS Z. Occurrence (c235). Which controls the count of flood occurrences is unresolved.

The percentage deductible mechanism operates on a "deductible factor shown on the Schedule of this endorsement," but that Schedule (c294) shows only flat dollar deductibles. The provision has no factor to apply.

The list of coverages for which no flood cover is provided includes Form RM1112, which is not among the forms listed on the POLICY INDEX or attached. The carve-out refers to a document outside the instrument.

The Schedule's location groups, per-occurrence limits, annual limits and deductibles are printed in detached columns, so it cannot be determined which of the $10,000,000, $5,000,000 and $1,000,000 limits, or which of the $50,000 and $100,000 deductibles, attaches to which Powder Tech location. The table is unreadable as drafted.

This insures loss from off-premises service interruption although GROUP A exclusion 9. (c109) excludes utility interference "if the failure occurs away from the covered location." The endorsement and the exclusion address the same event with opposite results.
